Noemi Giampaoli1,2 · Matteo Renghini1,2 Received: 19 May 2025 / Accepted: 20 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract In light of the European Central Bank’s (ECB) growing commitment to addressing climate change, this paper analyses how the ECB climate-related announcements affect banks’ stock market performance. Employing an event-study methodology on narrow event windows, we explore: (i) the banks’ response across the five an- nouncements, (ii) differences among European banks, Eurozone banks, and ECB- Supervised Institutions, and (iii) the type (positive or negative) and intensity of the response. Our findings reveal heterogeneous effects: the first, second, and fifth announcements trigger significant abnormal returns, partially discounted before- hand. Conversely, the third and fourth announcements exhibit limited effects. In all cases, effects dissipated rapidly. These results contribute to the understanding of how climate-related ECB communications interact with financial markets and bank stock returns, offering insights for investors assessing climate policy, for banks in managing climate-related risks, and for policymakers designing effective commu- nication strategies. Giampaoli, M. Renghini Introduction Climate change has become a systemic challenge for the financial sector, with grow- ing implications for banking supervision, credit risk, and financial stability. Central banks and regulators are increasingly integrating climate-related risks into their over- sight frameworks, using tools such as stress tests to assess financial institutions’ vul- nerability to both physical and transition risks (Henry et al. 2013; Borio et al. 2014). Among these, the European Central Bank (ECB) has taken a leading role in advanc- ing climate stress testing as a strategic instrument to guide banks’ alignment with sustainability standards and long-term risk management (Minton et al. 2014; Ellul and Yerramilli 2013). For instance, Schneider et al. (2025) examine how stress test- ing influences banks’ investment in risk management whereas Uslu and Çifçi (2025) show that sustainability-oriented strategies positively affect long-term risk appe- tite among institutional investors. Even earlier, Aven (2016) reviews foundational advances in risk assessment and management, highlighting the need for adaptive frameworks in the face of emerging environmental challenges. Meantime, the literature on stress testing has long recognized its dual role as a supervisory instrument and as a source of market-relevant information. Several stud- ies show that the results of traditional macro stress tests are capable of influencing stock valuations, particularly for riskier institutions (Petrella and Resti 2013; Fer- nandes et al. 2020). For example, Alves et al. (2015) find that two EBA stress tests - during the sovereign debt crisis - provided new and unanticipated information to equity markets, especially regarding the most vulnerable banks. Lazzari et al. (2017) demonstrate that the 2014 ECB Comprehensive Assessment surprised investors by revealing a stricter-than-expected supervisory stance, while Carboni et al. (2017) show that the formal launch of the Single Supervisory Mechanism was met with neg- ative market reactions for directly supervised banks. At the same time, concerns raise about the limits of stress tests as early warning tools, especially in periods of apparent financial stability, where vulnerabilities may remain hidden (Borio et al. 2014). By contrast, scholars have only recently started emphasizing the role of climate risk and ESG criteria in shaping credit policies, profitability, and resilience (Burana- trakul and Swierczek 2018; Chen et al. 2021; Caby et al. 2022; Galletta et al. 2022), with specific attention to the European regulatory context (Di Tommaso & Thorn- ton 2020; Toth et al. 2021; Cosma et al. 2022). Specifically, only a few recent studies focus on climate-related stress testing exercises. Torricelli et al. (2025) investigate investor reactions to the 2021 ECB economy-wide climate stress test and find that only the release of final quantitative results produces significant positive abnormal returns, as markets anticipated more adverse outcomes. Fiordelisi et al. (2025), in turn, show that both the announcement and results of the 2022 ECB climate stress test—focused on physical risks and the banking sector—generated negative market reactions, particularly among institutions more exposed to climate hazards. These studies underline the potential of climate stress tests to act as informational events, capable of reshaping investor expectations even in the absence of binding regulatory outcomes. Our analysis expands the existing literature in three ways. First, unlike Torricelli et al. (2025) and Fiordelisi et al. (2025), we focus on the announce- ment effects rather than the publication of stress test results, thereby timely assessing the broader signalling power of ECB communications. Second, we investigate the heterogeneity of announcements across banks, looking at all listed European banks, Eurozone-based banks, and ECB-supervised institutions (SIs). Third, we compare the effects of the announcements in terms of banks, sign and magnitude of the effects. We aim to answer the following research question: “Do central bank announce- ments in the climate change domain influence banks’ stock returns? If so, to what extent?“. To this end, we analyse five major ECB communications issued between 2020 and 2022 that explicitly address climate-related supervisory expectations or stress testing strategies. These announcements vary in timing, content, and regulatory assertiveness—from early declarations of methodological intent to more assertive statements of regulatory alignment—allowing us to test which aspects of climate change can trigger market sensitivity. Our empirical strategy combines an event study approach to detect short-term abnormal returns and differences pre, during and post the announcement day. The dataset comprises daily stock prices of 178 listed European banks – of which 106 Eurozone banks and 35 ECB-SIs – collected from Thomson Reuters DataStream. We restrict our sample to banks with complete time-series coverage from January 2, 2017, to June 24, 2022. Our findings indicate that not all announcements generate statistically significant reactions. In particular, the first (May 20, 2020), second (November 27, 2020), and fifth (March 14, 2022) announcements trigger the most pronounced and persistent abnormal returns, with the second and the fifth ones standing out as most impactful in terms of magnitude and statistical significance. By contrast, the third (November 22, 2021) and fourth (January 27, 2022) announcements produce limited responses by banks. This confirms that markets react more strongly when ECB communications shift from abstract guidance to concrete supervisory expectations or reveal tangible risks. Moreover, banks tend to react in anticipation of the most assertive announce- ments, with abnormal returns often emerging in the days preceding the event. These reactions are quite persistent when the announcements imply reputational or strategic consequences. However, volatility tends to normalize quickly, and banks experienc- ing significant movements in stock prices realign with the broader market within a few days. This paper builds on recent studies in stress tests and financial risk management by demonstrating that climate-related signals, such as those issued by the ECB, can influence banks’ behaviour. Our findings complement the insights of Uslu and Çifçi (2025) and Ma et al. (2025), showing that market reactions are influenced by climate-related requirements, which banks interpret as strategic imperatives—poten- tially enhancing their competitive positioning or exposing them to new risks. Specifically, this study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that ECB cli- mate-related announcements—particularly those perceived as credible and prescrip- tive—can work as powerful signals affecting market expectations and banks’ returns. In doing so, we extend the theoretical understanding of climate risk communication 2 Page 4 of 38 N. Giampaoli, M. Our results have also practical implications for central banks: even non-immediately-binding communications entail signalling effects that can influence banks behaviour and market sentiment. The first concerns the role of cli- mate change in the banking sector. The second stream relates to the role of stress tests and how the banking market reacts. Climate change and banking sector First, scholars have increasingly examined how integrate climate change and ESG into banks’ medium- and long-term strategies (Galletta et al. 2022). Furrer et al. (2012) early highlight that banks adjust their activities in line with climate-oriented strat- egies, while Buranatrakul and Swierczek (2018) compare these approaches across four macro-regions, finding that American and European banks are generally more aligned with climate requirements than their Asian counterparts. Meantime, Annichi- arico and Di Dio (2017) and Chen et al. (2021) explore how central banks incorporate climate change into monetary policy frameworks, noting that environmental factors can influence price dynamics and advocating for model revisions to account for these risks. Caby et al. (2022) investigate the effects of climate change on bank profitability in both emerging and developed economies, finding that tangible implications remain limited, despite the formal integration of climate considerations into bank strategies. At national level, evidence about climate change in the banking sector is more mixed. Kilic and Kuzey (2019) show that Turkish banks have not yet embedded cli- mate change into their business model strategies. Conversely, Paltrinieri et al. (2020) and Azmi et al. (2021) find a positive relationship between ESG scores and bank value for Islamic and emerging market banks, while El Khoury et al. (2021a); Khoury et al. (2021b) report a strong ESG–performance link in the Middle East, North Africa, and Turkey. In the European context, several studies assess the role of ESG in shap- ing bank activities (Di Tommaso & Thornton 2020; Toth et al. 2021; Chiaramonte et al. 2021; Cosma et al. 2022). Di Tommaso and Thornton (2020), alongside Gal- letta and Mazzù (2022) and Birindelli et al. (2022), analyse how ESG scores influ- ence banks’ risk appetite and value, linking these effects to board-level decisions. Toth et al. (2021) find that higher ESG performance reduces non-performing loans and, when paired with strong capital requirements, enhances credit provision to the real economy. Chiaramonte et al. (2021) corroborate these results, showing that ESG compliance supports financial stability during crises. Cosma et al. (2022) examine climate-related disclosures by European banks as a proxy for alignment with ESG Climate change, risks and ECB strategy: what is the effect on European… Page 5 of 38 2 policy, concluding that information remains only partially adequate and that corpo- rate social responsibility committees are key to long-term compliance. Beyond the strategic integration of ESG factors, recent studies have examined the direct financial implications of climate change for banks, with a growing focus on physical climate risks. The significance of such risks is underscored by broader empirical research. Specifically, physical climate risks such as natural disasters can weaken borrowers’ creditworthiness (Klomp 2014; Walker et al. 2023), reduce banks’ liquidity creation (Lee et al. 2022), and prompt higher lending margins and loan loss provisions (Do et al., 2023). Local branches, however, may help absorb shocks through post-disaster lending (Nguyen and Wilson 2020; Abedifar et al. 2024). Yet catastrophic events can substantially increase market volatility, depress capitaliza- tion, and widen the gap between book and market values (Brei et al. 2024; Wachter 2013), with insurance offering only partial mitigation (Zanin et al. 2024). Nonetheless, while climate change is increasingly recognised as a market risk dimension (Venturini 2022), empirical evidence withing the banking sector remains limited. Much of the focus has been on transition risk and lending patterns: Jung et al. (2023) report that banks committed to environmental limit exposure to high-risk sectors. Textual analyses by Zhang (2022) and Gong et al. (2022) further indicate that stock markets respond to changes in climate risk sentiment, though these studies are not bank-specific. Stress tests and market reaction Second, the literature on the role of supervisory stress tests in the banking sector provides robust evidence that such exercises, when well-designed and properly com- municated, convey novel and relevant information to financial markets. Several con- tributions document that stress test disclosure has led to stock price adjustments, especially for institutions perceived as riskier (Petrella and Resti 2013; Fernandes et al. 2020). For instance, during the European sovereign debt crisis, the EBA stress tests significantly impacted the stock returns of more vulnerable banks, revealing information not fully awaited by equity markets, but partially anticipated by credit default swap markets (Alves et al. 2015). Moreover, the 2014 ECB Comprehensive Assessment triggered a notable market reaction, as it conveyed a surprisingly strin- gent supervisory stance, resulting in negative abnormal returns, particularly for banks under the Single Supervisory Mechanism (Lazzari et al. 2017). Nonetheless, scholars also underscore the limitations of stress tests as early warn- ing tools, especially during periods of apparent market calm (Borio et al. 2014). With the increasing recognition of climate change as a source of financial instabil- ity, attention has turned toward the role of climate-related risks in banking supervision. Empirical studies have shown that climate-related events can convey market-relevant information (Capelle-Blancard and Petit 2019), yet the specific impact of climate stress tests remains largely underexplored. Torricelli et al. (2025) provide one of the first empirical assessments of market reactions to the ECB’s 2021 economy-wide climate stress test, focusing on euro area banks and non-financial corporations. Their event study analysis reveals three key findings: (i) the first announcement of the stress test methodology does not elicit significant market reactions, due to the quali- 2 Page 6 of 38 N. Building upon this foundation, Fiordelisi et al. (2025) investigate the market response to the ECB’s 2022 climate stress test, which for the first time focuses spe- cifically only on the banking sector and emphasizes physical risks. Using an event study and a dataset combining banks with regional indicators of climate-related physical risk (floods, landslides, and extreme temperatures), the authors show that investors react negatively to both the test’s announcement and the publication of its results, even if no direct impact on regulatory capital and no detailed disclosure for individual institutions occur. Gaps and contributions Despite the growing recognition of climate risks as a source of systemic fragility (Acharya et al. 2023; Monasterolo 2020) and the spread of studies in stress test (Tor- ricelli et al. 2025; Fiordelisi et al. 2025), further research is needed to clarify how banks adjust their behaviour in response to climate risk signals and whether bank- ing markets effectively internalize these risks. The recent ECB climate stress tests represent a unique opportunity to study these dynamics in a regulatory context, and the emerging empirical evidence suggests that investors are beginning to respond not only to disclosed exposures, but also to implicit signals embedded in supervisory climate risk assessments. This paper offers three contributions to the literature. First, it provides direct empirical evidence that the 2022 ECB climate stress test delivers incremental infor- mation to markets, even in the absence of disaggregated or capital-relevant dis- closures: specifically, ECB climate-related announcements can function as signals affecting the market. Second, we demonstrate that even non-binding communications from ECB can entail signalling effects that shape the market sentiment and affect banks’ behaviour. Finally, it reveals how market participants assess the risk exposure but also institutional commitments to responsible finance, echoing prior findings that link environmental performance to downside risk mitigation (Fiordelisi et al. 2023). This means that financial markets internalize to some extend supervisory expecta- tions over time. To assess the impact of ECB communications on banks’ stock prices in relation to cli- mate change, we select five specific announcements. These ones were chosen from a broader set of ECB publications dating back to 2017, including press releases, super- visory documents, and strategic communications. The selection has been guided by the objective of identifying announcements that are both explicitly climate-related and likely to convey new, market-relevant information. They also must serve as a signal of the ECB’s evolving expectations regarding banks’ awareness for climate challenges and their alignment with environmental sustainability standards. In par- ticular, the announcements have been chosen based on four criteria: (1) Explicit climate-related content: each announcement directly addresses climate- related financial risks or supervisory expectations in the context of banking supervision, risk management, or disclosure - distinguishing them from broader sustainability or ESG statements. (2) Strategic relevance: each announcement represents a key ambition in the ECB’s climate supervision roadmap, capturing the evolution from conceptual guidance to operational implementation. (3) Potential market value: each announcement contains new information or strate- gic signals that could influence market perceptions of banks’ climate risk expo- sure or future regulatory requirements. (4) Public visibility and accessibility: each announcement is publicly released by the ECB and widely disseminated, ensuring that information is unequivocally avail- able to the entire market. Based on these criteria, we select communications that represent distinct milestones in the ECB’s evolving climate supervisory strategy. These include five announce- ments, capturing distinct phases of policy development: – Initiation (May 20, 2020): first formal guidance draft sets the tone for future su- pervisory expectations. – Implementation (Nov 27, 2020): final guide marks transition from concept to action. – Assessment (Nov 22, 2021): first supervisory review reveals gaps and signals potential consequences (not yet applicable). – Operationalization (Jan 27, 2022): launch of climate stress test introduces up- coming evaluation tools. – Disclosure (Mar 14, 2022): first real assessment of banks’ climate reporting actu- ally highlights reputational and strategic risks. This progression allows us to study how different types of climate-related informa- tion - from conceptual to practical – affect banks’ stock returns. Table 5 complements this visual analysis by reporting the day-by-day t-tests and p-values, assessing the differences between significant RARs (and CRARs) and no-significant RARs (and CRARs), i.e., if these two groups are statistically different. While RARs capture the immediate, day-by- day banks’ reaction to ECB announcements, CRARs aggregate these effects over the entire event window, offering a broader view of the persistence and direction of the RARs’ dynamic. Considering both metrics allows us to assess not only whether banks react, but also how strongly and for how long these reactions unfold. The results in Fig. 2 indicate that banks with significant RARs tend to exhibit high volatility during the event window—both positive and negative. This volatility can be interpreted as a signal of uncertainty or perceived risk. ECB climate-related announcements often imply regulatory compliance costs, transition risks, and expo- sure to polluting sectors. However, the daily RARs are generally not statistically significant across the observed events. The only exception is the fifth announcement, related to the publication of the climate stress test results, which shows significant differences in the abnormal returns five times (columns 4–5 of Table 5). Further, we examine the CRARs over the event windows surrounding each ECB climate-related announcement. This approach allows us to assess the magnitude, direction, and persistence of the overall reactions, offering a comprehensive view of how banks internalize supervisory signals over time. Our results show that the first (May 20, 2020), second (November 27, 2020), and fifth (March 14, 2022) announce- ments generate the most significant and persistent CRARs, with statistical signifi- cance across the two groups of cumulated RARs (columns 6–9 of Table 5). The first announcement triggers a progressive and significant increase in CRARs among significantly reacting banks. From an initial value of − 1.00% on May 14, 2020, CRARs rises to + 6.73% by May 26, 2020, with high significance level before the announcement. This pattern suggests that the banking market interprets the announcement as a strategic shift in supervisory priorities, despite its non-binding nature, and begin pricing in future regulatory developments. The second announcement produces the strongest and most persistent reaction. CRARs reach + 30.58% on December 1, 2020, with highly significant and positive persistence on CRARs until December 2, 2020. This reflects the market’s recognition of the announcement’s regulatory centrality and its implications for risk manage- ment. Among the five events, this second announcement stands out as one of the most impactful in terms of statistical significance and marks a clear transition from conceptual guidance to concrete supervisory expectations, prompting a strong and sustained bank market response. Likewise, the fifth announcement elicits a strong and statistically significant reac- tion. RARs of banks moving and not-moving banks are proven to be statistically different in the announcement day (March 14, 2022), and CRARs begin rising in the days prior and peak at + 8.30% on March 17, 2022. This anticipatory and persistent response suggests that the market view the results of the stress test as credible signals of future supervisory tightening and structural adjustments, particularly for banks with inadequate climate risk disclosure. Specifically, we estimated abnormal returns as a difference between the return and its expected value–using the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)–and tested their statistical significance through the Boehmer et al. (1991) t-test. Our results show that the five ECB announcements have heterogeneous implica- tions, with the first (May 20, 2020), second (November 27, 2020), and fifth (March 14, 2022) announcements generating the most significant and persistent banks’ reactions. The analysis of cumulative abnormal returns (CRARs) further reveals that banks respond more strongly to announcements that convey concrete regulatory expecta- tions or reveal tangible risks, rather than to purely informational or methodological updates. Significant CRARs indicate that investors perceive the ECB’s supervisory direction as credible and strategically relevant. Meanwhile, positive CRARs sug- gests that investors interpret the ECB’s supervisory signals as supportive of long- term financial stability and effective climate risk management. In particular, the second announcement—marking the transition from conceptual guidance to concrete supervisory expectations—emerges as one of the most impact- ful. The fifth announcement, related to the publication of climate stress test results, triggers strong anticipatory reactions, especially among Eurozone banks and SIs. These findings are robust across different specifications of abnormal return as mean- adjusted returns (MAR), and market-adjusted returns (MKAR). These findings suggest that climate-related announcements by the ECB, while aimed at promoting sustainable finance, may also generate significant changes in the banking sector, or part of it (only the Eurozone or only the SIs). These findings have important policy implications. Policymakers should carefully consider the financial market repercussions of climate-related communication strate- gies, ensuring that announcements are clear, credible, and accompanied by concrete implementation plans for banks. Moreover, climate-related supervisory regulations should be designed in alignment with institutional governance frameworks. The observed heterogeneity in market reactions—especially among Eurozone banks and significant institutions (SIs)—suggests that tailored communication approaches may be necessary, accounting for differences in regulatory exposure and systemic relevance. To conclude, this paper lays the foundation for future studies. Future research could consider the entire channel of policy transmission by the ECB, examining how climate-related supervisory signals unfold effects through the financial system. Schol- ars should explore the long-term effects of climate-related supervisory announce- ments and their interaction with macroeconomic conditions, regulatory changes, and investor behaviour. Additionally, the development of predictive models to anticipate market responses to climate policy signals could support more effective and less dis- ruptive communication strategies. Given the highlighted policy implications, potential studies could also explore not only the banks’ profitability side but also the cost of adjusting to climate-related requirements, especially in response to ECB guidelines. Policy frameworks should also consider the asymmetry in investor responses and the reputational dynamics triggered by climate disclosures, particularly in the context of evolving sustainability standards. JSON: Name: ecb_climate_eventstudy Title: Event-study analysis of the impact of ECB climate-related announcements on listed European banks' stock returns Short Hypothesis: ECB climate-related announcements cause statistically significant abnormal stock returns for listed European banks within a nine-day event window (−4,+4 trading days) around each announcement. Related Work: Prior research applies event-study methods and stress-test disclosure analysis to measure how supervisory communications affect financial institutions' equity prices, typically using CAPM-based abnormal returns, market- and mean-adjusted benchmarks, and short event windows. More recent work has extended this framework to climate stress tests, showing that publication of stress-test results can move markets, but existing studies emphasize either final results or economy-wide exercises and often focus on limited country samples or on aggregate market indices. Limitations across the literature include (1) emphasis on results rather than announcement signalling effects, (2) inconsistent abnormal-return specifications and limited robustness to event-induced variance and cross-correlation, (3) inadequate subgroup analysis (e.g., Eurozone vs non-Eurozone vs supervised institutions), and (4) insufficient treatment of anticipation effects, confounding news and alternative market proxies. Abstract: This research pipeline tests whether ECB climate-related supervisory announcements function as market signals that produce abnormal equity returns for listed European banks. Using a narrow event-study design, the approach estimates CAPM-based abnormal returns and alternative benchmarks (mean- and market-adjusted returns) for 178 euro-denominated listed banks over the period 2017–2022 around five ECB climate-announcement dates. Analysis will quantify the incidence, sign, magnitude and persistence of abnormal returns for full and subgroup samples (Eurozone banks and ECB supervised institutions), and contrast announcement effects against background market movements and alternative event-window specifications. Main contributions are (i) isolating announcement signalling effects separate from final-stress-test disclosures, (ii) providing a robustness protocol addressing event-induced variance, anticipation, and multiple benchmarks, and (iii) delivering subgroup evidence on heterogeneity in market response. Expected outcomes are a reproducible assessment of which announcement types elicit market reactions and how those reactions vary by bank category. Experiments: Datasets: daily closing prices and returns for 178 euro-denominated listed European banks (Thomson Reuters Datastream), MSCI EMU Commercial Banks index (market proxy), sample period 2 Jan 2017–24 Jun 2022. Event set: five ECB announcements (dates: 2020-05-20, 2020-11-27, 2021-11-22, 2022-01-27, 2022-03-14). Preprocessing: restrict to banks with complete series 2017-01-02 onward; compute daily log returns; align trading calendars. Baselines: CAPM abnormal returns (RAR) using OLS-estimated alpha/beta over estimation window (full sample start to 7 trading days before event), mean-adjusted returns (MAR), market-adjusted returns (MKAR). Primary tests: compute RAR, MAR, MKAR for event window t = -4..+4; aggregate cumulative abnormal returns (CRAR); apply Boehmer–Musumeci–Poulsen t-test to adjust for event-induced variance; report cross-sectional counts and proportions of banks with statistically significant ARs at 5% and 1% levels. Subsamples: (a) all European banks, (b) Eurozone banks, (c) ECB-supervised institutions (SIs). Robustness and comparisons: (1) alternative market proxies (e.g., broad EMU index, national banking indices), (2) alternative estimation windows (−250..−31, −500..−31), (3) alternative event windows (−1..+1, −2..+2, −10..+10) to test anticipation and persistence, (4) permutation test: randomly assign pseudo-event dates (N=1,000) to estimate empirical null distribution of CRAR, (5) bootstrap clustered standard errors and cross-sectional block-bootstrap for p-values, (6) ablation: drop pre-event days (test purely contemporaneous effect), (7) Fama–MacBeth and panel regressions controlling for bank characteristics (market cap, leverage, ESG/disclosure proxies, country fixed effects) to explain heterogeneity, (8) multiple-testing adjustment (Benjamini–Hochberg) for cross-sectional significance. Evaluation metrics: proportion of banks with significant ARs, mean and median AR and CRAR per group, effect size (AR relative to pre-event volatility), duration until reversion to market baseline (days until bank return correlation with index returns returns to pre-event level), and robustness of inferences under permutation/bootstrapping. Deliverables: tables of daily ARs and CRARs, subgroup comparisons, regression outputs, permutation p-values, and sensitivity plots across specifications. Risk Factors and Limitations: Event identification risks: announcements may coincide with other macro or firm-specific news producing confounding effects. Anticipation and leakage: markets may price announcements before official release, complicating causal attribution within the chosen window. Statistical issues: event-induced variance and cross-sectional correlation can inflate type I error; multiple-testing across banks and windows increases false discovery risk. Data biases: survivorship and selection biases from excluding banks with incomplete series; thin trading and non-synchronous trading distort daily returns for small-cap banks. Market-proxy choice: results depend on the index used to estimate normal returns and betas. Subgroup power: sample sizes for SIs or country subsets may be small, reducing statistical power. External validity: findings limited to euro-denominated listed European banks over 2017–2022 and may not generalize to non-listed banks, other regions, or different regulatory regimes. Measurement: ECB announcement content heterogeneity (guidance vs operational tests vs disclosures) complicates homogeneous effect interpretation. Computational: bootstrap and permutation procedures require substantial compute for 1,000+ iterations on cross-sectional panels.
